SECTION: Methodology (Pages 24-31)

TOPICS: survey design, sampling methods, weighting procedures, data collection, population definitions, margin of error, dual-frame surveys, reference sources

TEXT_EVIDENCE:
- The analysis is based on two Pew Research Center national surveys (Page 24)
- The 2015 National Survey of Latinos was conducted from Oct. 21 through Nov. 30, 2015, with a sample of 1,500 adults (Page 24)
- A second survey was conducted from Nov. 11, 2015, through Feb. 7, 2016, with a sample of 401 adults (Page 24)
- Both surveys were conducted by SSRS for Pew Research Center (Page 24)
- Americans of Hispanic ancestry are defined as two groups: self-identified Hispanics and non-Hispanics with a Hispanic parent or grandparent (Page 24)
- Screening questions for self-identified Hispanics include: "Are you Hispanic or Latino?" and "Just to confirm, are you, yourself of Hispanic or Latino origin or descent?" (Page 24)
- Screening questions for non-Hispanics with Hispanic ancestry include: "Are you of Hispanic or Latino origin or descent?" and questions about parents' origins (Page 24)
- The combined sample weights were set so that self-identified Hispanics made up 89% and those with Hispanic ancestry but not identifying as such made up 11% (Page 25)
- Self-identified Hispanics account for 16% of the non-institutionalized adult population (37.8 million) (Page 25)
- Individuals with Hispanic ancestry but not self-identifying make up just under 2% of all U.S. adults (4.9 million) (Page 25)
- The 2015 National Survey of Latinos included 1,500 Latino respondents aged 18 and older (Page 25)
- The survey was conducted from Oct. 21 through Nov. 30, 2015 (Page 25)
- For the full sample, 705 respondents were U.S. born and 795 were foreign born (Page 25)
- The margin of error for the total sample is ±3.3 percentage points at 95% confidence (Page 25)
- 679 respondents (45%) were surveyed in Spanish, and 821 (55%) were interviewed in English (Page 25)

- The combined sample weights were set so that self-identified Hispanics made up 89% and those with Hispanic ancestry but not identifying as such made up 11% (Page 25)
- Self-identified Hispanics account for 16% of the non-institutionalized adult population (37.8 million) (Page 25)
- Individuals with Hispanic ancestry but not self-identifying make up just under 2% of all U.S. adults (4.9 million) (Page 25)
- The 2015 National Survey of Latinos included 1,500 Latino respondents aged 18 and older (Page 25)
- The survey was conducted from Oct. 21 through Nov. 30, 2015 (Page 25)
- For the full sample, 705 respondents were U.S. born and 795 were foreign born (Page 25)
- The margin of error for the total sample is ±3.3 percentage points at 95% confidence (Page 25)
- 679 respondents (45%) were surveyed in Spanish, and 821 (55%) were interviewed in English (Page 25)
- Any person ages 18 or older who said they were of Latino origin or descent was eligible (Page 25)
- The study used a dual-frame landline/cellular telephone design (Page 26)
- The total sample consisted of 449 landline interviews and 1,051 cellphone interviews, totaling 1,500 completed interviews (Page 26)
- The study employed a stratified sampling design with six strata to oversample areas with higher densities of Latino residents (Page 26)
- The sample was generated using random digit dial (RDD), with numbers subdivided based on Spanish surnames for administrative purposes (Page 26)
- Landline and cellphone samples were provided by Marketing Systems Group (MSG) (Page 26)
- MSG's GENESYS system was used to generate the cell phone sample, which was divided into High and Medium strata (Page 26)

To ensure the highest possible coverage of the eligible population, the study employed a dual-frame landline/cellular telephone design. The sample consisted of a landline sampling frame (yielding 449 completed interviews) and a cellphone sampling frame (1,051 interviews). Both the landline and cellphone sampling frames used a stratified sampling design, oversampling areas with higher densities of Latino residents. Overall the study employed six strata. Landline and cellphone samples were provided by Marketing Systems Group (MSG). For the landline sampling frame, the sample was compared with InfoUSA and Experian landline household databases, and phone numbers associated with households that included persons with known Latino surnames were subdivided into a surname stratum. The remaining, unmatched and unlisted landline sample was used to generate a stratum with a high incidence of Latinos, based upon the share of Latinos in the sample telephone exchange. It is important to note that the existence of a surname stratum does not mean the survey was exclusively a surname sample design. The sample is random digit dial (RDD), with the randomly selected telephone numbers divided by whether or not they were found to be associated with a Spanish surname. This was done to ease administration by allowing for more effective assignment of interviewers and labor hours, as well as increase the efficiency of the sample. MSG's GENESYS sample generation system was used to generate cell phone sample, which was divided into High and Medium strata, based upon the share of Latinos in the sample telephone area code.
